newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian markets fall on Yeltsin operation news.
newsitem.headline: Russian markets fall on Yeltsin operation news.

text.p: Russian stocks and bonds fell Monday on news that a heart operation on President Boris Yeltsin may be delayed for up to two months or abandoned altogether.
Share prices fell by up to 7 percent, and Treasury bill prices dropped by up to 5 percent as the markets faced up to the possibility of a prolonged period of political uncertainty.
Renat Akchurin, the surgeon chosen to conduct the operation on Yeltsin, said on Sunday the 65-year-old leader could wait another 1-1/2 to two months and might not have it at all.
The Kremlin had no comment on Monday.
"Investors should begin briskly preparing for the post-Yeltsin era," said Moscow-based investment bank Renaissance Capital in its weekly Moscow comment.
This need not provoke panic or hysteria, but investors needed to consider how a transfer of power would take place and who likely successors would be if Yeltsin died or stepped down, it said.
Martin Diggle of Brunswick said the markets still believed Yeltsin would undergo an operation in the coming months.
"The worst thing that could happen for the market would be fore Yeltsin to be too weak to have the operation," he said.
"Then there would be a continuation of the uncertainty and that's the last thing the market wants."
Stocks opened up to 5 percent lower and continued to drift down in moderate volumes on selling mainly from Western investors.
"A lot of people are calling in, people are concerned and want to know what's happening and there are more sellers than buyers," Diggle said.
Investors wishing to buy were waiting in the hope of lower prices this week, he said.
Traders said prices would go down further.
"The fall will continue, but there is a floor of 10 to 15 percent at current levels," said Pavel Gronbjerg, joint head equities trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Diggle said stock prices would now depend completely on the news on Yeltsin's health.
Treasury bill and government bond prices fell by up to nearly 5 percent on the news, as investors switched out of ruble instruments.
